extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, biologists, and educated readers interested in evolutionary theory (19th-century scientific audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for recognizing, distinguishing, and explaining sexual selection and its effects across animal taxa, including how to separate sexual from natural selection and what evidence supports sexual selection acting on particular characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs of reproduction that necessarily differ between the sexes (the reproductive glands and directly reproductive structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are contrasted with secondary characters; some structures graduate into primary characters and may be hard to distinguish. Examples: reproductive glands; receptacles for ova in certain male fishes; organs for nourishing young (mammary glands) are often sex-limited but relate to reproductive function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary sexual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual differences not directly connected with the act of reproduction, e.g. greater size, strength, weapons, ornaments, song, or scent-producing glands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes structures for finding, reaching, or holding females, ornaments to allure females, weapons for fighting rivals, vocal/instrumental contrivances, and glands emitting odours. These characters often serve only to give a reproductive advantage and are the principal focus of sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and core criterion of sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection depends on the advantage which certain individuals have over others of the same sex and species solely in respect of reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The defining test: if a character gives an advantage in mating relative to conspecific rivals (and not primarily in survival), it can be attributed to sexual selection. Traits that increase success in acquiring mates or preventing rivals from mating are candidates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing sexual from natural selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection differs from natural selection in that it acts through advantages in reproductive success rather than advantages in survival or ordinary life functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a trait's chief effect is to give one individual an advantage over another in pairing (even if it harms survival), it is sexual selection. Where a trait serves mainly for ordinary life (food-getting, escaping predators), natural selection is the likely cause. Many cases are ambiguous and both forces may act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of action: male–male competition (rivalry, weapons, prehensile organs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits developed to enable males to fight with, drive away, or hold off rivals, including weapons of offence/defence and prehensile appendages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: claspers of male worms, specialized legs and antennae in oceanic crustaceans for holding females, rasplike surfaces on males that coil around females. Such structures may be perfected because they prevent female escape or displacement by rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner of action: female choice (preference-driven traits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Traits evolved because females preferentially mate with males exhibiting them (ornaments, bright colours, song, displays, odours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual selection by female choice can produce gaudy colouring, ornamentation, vocal or instrumental courtship, and scent glands. Darwin stresses that many characters (colour, hairiness, form of features) are of a kind that might have been expected to arise via female choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of sex ratios and mating systems (excess of males, polygamy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The numerical relation of the sexes and the mating system (e.g., polygamy) strongly influence the intensity and direction of sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An excess of males and polygamous systems increase male–male competition and strengthen sexual selection on males; Darwin provides a supplement on proportions of sexes and relates sex ratio to natural selection as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency for males to be principally modified
rubrics_metrics.description: In many species the male alone is generally more modified through sexual selection than the female.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons include male–male competition and female choice, but Darwin acknowledges exceptions where females are modified (e.g., some bees, or where females are the foragers and thus possess special organs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Male eagerness and behavioral asymmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: Males often exhibit greater eagerness or active pursuit of females, which biases selection toward male traits that increase mating success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This behavioral asymmetry contributes to the direction of selection—competition, display, or persistence may be selected in males. Darwin notes the importance of the male's behavior in acquiring mates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male variability as a substrate for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Greater variability in males supplies the raw material upon which sexual selection can act more readily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If males are more variable, sexual selection can more quickly fix advantageous mating traits in male lineages; variability interacts with choice and competition to produce pronounced sexual dimorphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inheritance limited by sex, age, or season
rubrics_metrics.description: Inheritance of traits may be expressed only at corresponding periods of life, during certain seasons, or limited to one sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin emphasizes that sex-limited inheritance explains why some traits appear only in one sex or at particular life stages; this affects how sexual selection shapes sexually dimorphic traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relations between different forms of inheritance
rubrics_metrics.description: Different modes of inheritance (sex-limited, age-limited, seasonal) interact and influence the development of sexual characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding how inheritance operates across sexes and life stages is crucial for attributing traits to sexual selection vs other causes; Darwin discusses these relations qualitatively rather than providing a formal genetic model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons why one sex and the young are not modified
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations for why sexual selection often fails to modify one sex (usually females) and juveniles include different selective roles, costs, and the timing/expression of inherited traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait confers mating advantage only to adult males, it may not appear in females or juveniles because of sex-limited inheritance or because it would be disadvantageous in those life stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of functional vs reproductive explanations for sex-differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish differences caused by natural selection for different habits of life from those caused by sexual selection for reproductive advantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: in species where sexes have different ecological roles (female pollen-collecting apparatus in bees, Huia beak differences), natural selection for life-history tasks explains differences rather than sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlated development as a confounding factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Some traits may appear due to correlated development with other selected characters rather than direct selection on the trait itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin gives examples (muscular development and supra-orbital ridges; skin odour correlated with colour) and cautions that correlated changes can mislead inference about causes; compare with domesticated animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of use/disuse and direct environmental action
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct action of conditions and use/disuse often fail to account satisfactorily for the observed sexual and racial differences—these mechanisms are usually insufficient alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues that direct environmental effects, continued use of parts, or simple correlation cannot fully explain many differences (e.g., between human races); sexual selection is proposed as a more powerful explanatory agent for certain characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits indicative of sexual selection (weapons, ornaments, song, odour glands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific classes of traits—weapons, ornamentation, vocal/instrumental displays, scent glands—are likely products of sexual selection when they function in rivalry or mate attraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When such traits primarily affect mating success (e.g., display to attract females, structures to defeat rivals), they should be evaluated as sexual-selection products. Darwin lists these classes as especially likely to arise by sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative anatomy and development as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative anatomical and embryological similarities and differences (e.g., brain structure and order of sulci development) provide evidence for common descent and for assessing whether particular traits are derived or ancestral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin uses development/order of sulci and comparative convolution patterns across primates to argue continuity between human and ape brains; developmental congruence supports evolutionary hypotheses and can inform whether a trait is likely due to sexual selection vs inheritance from ancestors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic value of highly variable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters that are highly variable within a group have little taxonomic (classification) value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: presence/absence or degree of development of certain sulci (external perpendicular fissure) varies within humans and apes and therefore is unreliable as a defining taxonomic character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection as a partial but not exclusive explanation for human racial differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual selection can account for many human differences (colour, hairiness, features), but not necessarily all; unexplained residual variation may be due to spontaneous variation fixed by other agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin warns not to over-claim: some racial differences may arise by sexual selection, others by long-continued intercrossing of slight spontaneous variations or unknown agencies; intellectual and moral faculties are exceptions where selection for function is obvious.
